title: Industrial Process Control Platform
summary: Creative Navy worked on an in-development process control platform for automated machining cells. The documented engagement includes a separately scoped UX audit, six one-week design sprints, an ongoing twelve-month retainer at two weeks per month, and a second touchscreen control product workstream.
keyFacts: The client is anonymised as a European industrial automation vendor whose process control software coordinates machining cells.
The engagement has three stages: an initial UX audit, a six-sprint design block, and an ongoing twelve-month retainer at two weeks per month.

Creative Navy-recorded engagement facts include a five-person team, four competitors benchmarked, five personas from direct research sessions, and in-situ operator observation at the client's demonstration facility.
Creative Navy delivered 48 screens during the six-sprint design block and 46 further screens during the retainer to date, for 94 total screens recorded in the engagement evidence.
The platform is in development and the case evidence does not establish production, throughput, efficiency, error-rate, commercial, or market outcomes.
Components documented and marked ready for development have been implemented, but this is not evidence of product outcome because the platform is still in development.

bodySections.heading: Anonymised Industrial Process Control Platform for Machining Cells
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Creative Navy worked with a European industrial automation vendor whose process control software coordinates automated machining cells. The platform tracks which physical workpiece is on which pallet, which pallet is in which location, and how machines can continue running without unnecessary manual intervention.

The engagement is recorded in three stages. Creative Navy first conducted a separately scoped UX audit of the existing platform. Creative Navy then completed six one-week design sprints covering parts and projects and the node screen. Creative Navy is now working on a twelve-month retainer at two weeks per month, with a parallel touchscreen control product scoped as a separate workstream.

bodySections.heading: Operating Reality of the Automated Machining Cell
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The process control platform coordinates a cell of CNC machines, storage magazines, workbenches, a loading station, wheeled trolleys, and a loading robot on a rail. The client refers to a cell as a node. One operator is typically responsible for one cell per shift.

Work moves through the cell on pallets. A raw block of metal is clamped to a pallet, the pallet carries an RFID chip, and the robot moves pallets between magazines and machine chucks. Upstream, a CAM engineer turns a CAD model into an NC program and a workflow. Downstream, an operator sets up the physical blank, has it measured on a coordinate measuring machine, and releases it into the cell.

The operating problem is that the system's digital model can drift from physical reality. A pallet can be moved by hand, a door can be opened, or a workpiece can be mounted differently from the recorded state. The interface therefore has to support reconciliation between the digital record and the physical truth through visual confirmation, RFID scanning, or robot-read storage scans.

Manual intervention has an operational cost because entering the cell stops production. The safety fence shuts everything down when a person walks in. The interface therefore has to help the operator anticipate and batch interventions rather than treat each intervention as an isolated screen event.

Creative Navy-observed operating conditions included standing-height interfaces bolted to individual machines, mixed daylight and industrial lighting with glare, medium ambient noise, oil and metal swarf, and aisles roughly one person wide.

bodySections.heading: Expert Review Findings on Colour, Legibility, Consistency, and State Visibility
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy conducted a heuristic expert review of the existing platform in a demonstration environment. The review covered parts and projects management, part creation, the cell overview, the manual preset workplace, the setup workplace, storage inspection, the robot page, and the monitoring view.

The central audit finding was that one accent colour carried six meanings. The corporate red signalled brand identity, primary action, selected table row, active filter, current navigation location, and error. This meant that an urgent machine fault used the same colour family as ordinary selection.

Two reviewed examples made the state-visibility problem concrete. A storage unit tile showed a green header band for transporting and a solid red icon for selected, with no legend on screen and only a subtle border-weight change as an additional cue. In the alarms table, an error row and a selected row were both solid red in the same table at the same time.

Creative Navy-recorded audit evidence also identified legibility and consistency failures. Button text was recorded from the design file inspector as 10px Noto Sans, line-height 100%, uppercase with wide tracking, on screens read while standing and at distance in a daylit hall. The audit found six different ways of showing selection, five coexisting date formats, mixed units within a single column, navigation that changed between screens, four names for one machine, and primary actions relocating mid-task.

bodySections.heading: Configurable Roles Made Information Architecture a Constraint-Respecting Problem
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The hardest structural problem was that Creative Navy could not assume a fixed information architecture. The client's customers configure user groups themselves, choose which interface components each group needs, and that selection generates the group's navigation.

The configuration space covered five company archetypes, from a single-operator shop to a large corporation with eleven distinct operator groups across six components. Roles also change over time: a setup-dedicated operator may leave, and a preset operator may need to absorb both tasks without accepting two separate computers.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treated this as a constraint respecting and organic system building problem. The design work had to produce a chassis that stayed coherent under customer-assembled configurations, while making each component legible alone and in combination.

This information-architecture constraint is more specific than a general industrial interface problem. The dominant design challenge was a mutable, multi-role operating environment in which the product had to adapt to different organisational structures without losing state visibility or task clarity.

bodySections.heading: Research, Domain Learning, and Requirements Artefacts During the Six-Sprint Design Block
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy-recorded research during the six-sprint design block produced five personas from direct research sessions, covering six individuals across three role types. Creative Navy also observed operators in situ at the client's demonstration facility, benchmarked four competitors, and used hands-on access to a demonstration environment for domain learning.

The six-sprint block covered two areas: parts and projects, which formed the upstream engineering surface, and the node screen, which formed the operator surface. Creative Navy compressed research, requirements, exploration, structural design, and visual design into this block.

A shared requirements table was co-authored with the client screen by screen. The table captured purpose, content, actions, priority, Creative Navy's open questions, and the client's answers. The artefact made assumptions explicit and visible, matching the blanks phenomenon described in Creative Navy's terminology.

Creative Navy's design work used greyscale structural exploration before visual design, with a UI brief agreed during the block. The six-sprint block delivered 48 screens, recorded as an engagement fact rather than an outcome claim.

bodySections.heading: Design Response to Status Ambiguity, Action Hierarchy, Panels, and Empty States
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method connected headline audit findings to identifiable design responses. The strongest design evidence in this case is traceability from demonstrated interface problem to demonstrated design response, rather than a deployed outcome.

Red was reserved for brand, error states, and destructive actions only. Primary actions became dark or neutral. Status communication moved to a seven-state taxonomy covering ready, warning, processing, done, error, transport, and end-of-life. Each state used a distinct hue, a text label, and an icon, so colour was not the only carrier of meaning.

Creative Navy specified action hierarchy rules for entity panels. The transport action is primary when the robot can move the item, the linking action is primary when it cannot, and unlink is always secondary. This replaced inconsistent button placement and unclear action priority with a documented rule.

Creative Navy also standardised the modal pattern, using secondary action on the left and primary action on the right. A single side panel pattern included specified default and minimum widths and documented default, hover, focused, and pressed states. Empty states were written for list views and storage positions rather than leaving blank cards unexplained.

A documented status timeline component distinguished future, current, and completed steps. The component marked automatic versus manual transitions and surfaced preconditions on hover. Filters, sorting, and column controls were placed consistently in a fixed position.

bodySections.heading: RFID Linking Feedback Answered a Physical Visibility Problem
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's design response for RFID linking is a clear trace from research observation to interface specification. A node operator reported that the RFID linking step gave no audio response, was visually too small, and did not provide feedback when the screen was not visible from the loading station.

The design response specified distinct audio feedback patterns for scanning. The scan dialog distinguished a first scan from a second scan and separated valid from invalid pallet signals. It also distinguished scanning an empty chuck, an occupied chuck, an empty loading station, and an occupied loading station.

This design decision addressed a physical operating condition rather than a purely visual interface issue. In the client's facility, each operator screen is bolted to its own machine, and an operator cannot rely on reading a screen across the hall. The cell overview therefore functions as a digital equivalent of a stack light: it gives a readable state overview in a setting where the operator may not be standing at the relevant machine.

bodySections.heading: Assistance Layer Preserved Operator Authorship While Separating Notifications From Instructions
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's retainer work later included an operator instructions layer. The design was shaped by a research finding that operators express strong ownership of their cell, referring to it as their node, and can resist being instructed by software.

Creative Navy's design separated notification from instruction. A notification describes what has already happened and is acknowledged. An instruction describes what the operator should do next and is completed. This distinction preserved a clearer role for the operator while still allowing the system to support task execution.

Instructions were grouped by day, carried inline links to the entities involved, and could be filtered by type, machine, timeline, and location. A batching panel grouped related manual interventions in one storage unit into a single instruction, so the operator could make one trip rather than respond to many separate items.

The batching design is tied to the documented operating reality that entering the cell stops production.

bodySections.heading: Retainer Work, Component Documentation, and Implemented Development-Ready Components
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's ongoing retainer covers rolling screen-by-screen work at two weeks per month over twelve months. Retainer work includes storage views, machine detail, robot detail, workflow creation and editing, planning, manual preset, setup workplace, and an operator instructions layer.

Creative Navy-recorded delivery during the retainer includes 46 further screens to date, bringing the recorded total to 94 screens across the six-sprint design block and retainer. Deliverables now include written component documentation paired with prototypes and marked ready for development.

Components marked ready for development have been implemented. This is a supported engagement fact and adoption fact, but it is not a product outcome claim.

The component documentation reflects progressive specification in the retainer. Design decisions were not only represented in prototypes; they were documented in a form that development teams could use.

bodySections.heading: Touchscreen Control Workstream Required a Different Interaction Layer
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy also scoped a separate touchscreen control product for a small touchscreen device with hardware buttons alongside desktop use. Creative Navy offered one-, two-, and three-sprint options, and the client selected the three-sprint option.

Creative Navy argued that a single sprint would create structurally incomplete foundations and hidden downstream cost. The risk described in the scoping work was that teams would either work around unresolved decisions or carry unresolved decisions forward as design debt.

The technical judgement was that most desktop platform components could not be reused directly at touchscreen scale. Touch targets, spacing, typography, layout density, and navigation differ between desktop and touchscreen use. The design goal was therefore a coherent extension of the design system, not direct reuse of the desktop interaction layer.

bodySections.heading: Regulatory and Alarm-Management Context for the Platform
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The client's functional specification named the NIS2 Directive and the Cyber Resilience Act as drivers for the platform's user-identification requirements. This is engagement context for the platform's requirements.

The platform's alarm work should be read against ISA-18.2 and IEC 62682 as relevant alarm-management context. The alarm view contained severity, source classification, and fault codes, which is where a rationalisation discipline would begin.

Creative Navy's role was design work on control software interfaces and workflows.
